Scope and boundaries

Methodology

The audit was performed by the QSI engine 1.3.0. Each analyzer emits facts (rule, parameters, evidence); finding texts are generated from the rule catalog. Methodology sources are listed under "Sources and normative documents".

Prioritization uses an explainable weighted model (severity, exploitability, exposure, confidentiality/integrity/availability impact weighted by the "Crypto exchange, custodian or wallet" profile, asset criticality, urgency, ease of remediation) with a confidence multiplier. CVSS v3.1 is applied only to technical vulnerabilities with a defined vector. Long-term quantum risks use Mosca's inequality; their severity is capped at Medium and they are never presented as exploitable vulnerabilities.

Finding classes: confirmed technical vulnerability; known vulnerable component (a dependency version named in an advisory; whether the affected code is reachable is assessed separately, and a component confirmed by review becomes a vulnerability); confirmed configuration error; potential cryptographic risk; long-term post-quantum risk; improvement recommendation; insufficient data. Heuristic findings are marked preliminary; analyst decisions are shown next to the findings.

Architecture overview

Static review of the source tree stellar-core at 362dbc5184c5fdc0d6e898f3046639dc5e2a4f32. 3388 files analysed; of 27064 files, 5182 are test, fuzzing, benchmark or example code and were left out, 16879 are not read by any analyzer, 0 exceed the per-file limit and 1615 did not fit the total limit. Files no analyzer reads include: .clang-format, .claude/skills/adding-a-new-skill/SKILL.md, .claude/skills/configuring-the-build/SKILL.md, .claude/skills/high-level-code-review/SKILL.md, .claude/skills/low-level-code-review/SKILL.md. Because the total limit bound, this inventory covers 3388 of 27064 candidate files (12%) and is a sample of the tree rather than a reading of it; a different limit gives a different figure. Files it could not fit include: lib/tracy/server/TracyMicroArchitecture.cpp, src/rust/soroban/p24/soroban-env-host/src/host/metered_vector.rs, src/rust/soroban/p24/soroban-env-host/src/host/prng.rs, src/rust/soroban/p24/soroban-env-host/src/host/trace.rs, src/rust/soroban/p24/soroban-env-host/src/host/trace/fmt.rs. 765 files in build-output or dependency-cache directories (.git, .hg, .venv, __pycache__, build, dist, node_modules, target, vendor, venv) were not read. 2628 files come from directories a .gitmodules pins and are read as shipped source rather than skipped as a dependency cache: lib/asio (596), lib/tracy (344), lib/gperftools (240), lib/libsodium (240). No requests were sent to the owner's systems.

QSI-2026-19587 · RNG-WEAK-KEYGENHigh

Non-cryptographic generator next to key or seed generation in src/crypto/SecretKey.h

Potential cryptographic riskConfidence: Mediumpreliminary — requires further verification

'random()' at line 59, within a few lines of 'SecretKey' (1 occurrence(s)).

Affected asset
src/crypto/SecretKey.h:keygen
Data source
src/crypto/SecretKey.h
Detection method
Regular-expression matching of language-specific API patterns.
Analyzer
entropy 1.3.0 · 2026-11-06 16:13 UTC
Priority score
38.8 / 100 (Crypto exchange, custodian or wallet)
CVSS v3.1
not applicable

Potential impact

Mnemonics, seeds or private keys drawn from such a generator can be enumerated from its small internal state: Milk Sad (CVE-2023-39910, mt19937 behind 'bx seed') and Trust Wallet (CVE-2023-31290) lost funds this way.

Reproduction steps

Open line 59 in the supplied file src/crypto/SecretKey.h and inspect the quoted lines (see evidence).

Evidence

file_excerpt · src/crypto/SecretKey.h · line 59 · SHA-256 bc0ec8d966e45191… · File f482c40875d15be5…
   57 | 
   58 |     // Create a new, random secret key.
   59 |     static SecretKey random();
   60 | 
   61 |     // Measure the speed of sign-and-verify ops.

Limitations of the check

Heuristic pattern match on source text without data-flow analysis. The usage context (security-relevant or not) must be confirmed manually; treat as preliminary.

Recommendation

Use the platform CSPRNG (secrets, os.urandom, crypto.getRandomValues, crypto/rand, SecureRandom, OsRng) or a hardware TRNG for every key, seed and mnemonic.

Retest procedure

Re-scan the source and review the call sites listed in the evidence.

CWE-338 — Use of Cryptographically Weak Pseudo-Random Number Generator (PRNG); CVE-2023-39910 — Libbitcoin Explorer 'bx seed' entropy (Milk Sad): mt19937 limits it to 32 bits; CVE-2023-31290 — Trust Wallet Core: 32 bits of mnemonic entropy (mt19937 seeded with one 32-bit value)

Post-quantum assessment

Data/key lifetime x1010
Migration time y55
Assumed years to CRQC z8 (early)8

Planning assumptions: x for key establishment, x for signatures, y are the defaults of the risk profile “Crypto exchange, custodian or wallet”, not the client's figures; with the client's actual lifetimes the verdict can change.

Post-quantum maturity: Level 1 of 4 — post-quantum code present, not wired

  • A post-quantum library is declared as a dependency
  • Classical only — key wrapping and data encryption at rest: X25519 (1 file(s))

Next step: Wire the existing post-quantum primitive into a critical path (key wrapping or the channel) behind a hybrid construction, and test interoperability.

Levels: 0 none; 1 present, not wired; 2 in use outside the critical paths; 3 hybrid in a critical path; 4 post-quantum by default in the critical paths (root of trust, key wrapping, channel key exchange). Judged from code and manifests.

What the quantum-vulnerable algorithms do

RoleAlgorithms (files)IDFirst step
key wrapping and data encryption at restX25519 (1)QSI-2026-19581Wrap keys with ML-KEM or a hybrid KEM (X25519 + ML-KEM-768) and re-wrap the stored keys; data that may already have been copied needs its own assessment
transaction and message signingEd25519 (12), ECDSA (8)QSI-2026-19579, QSI-2026-19583Follow each chain's post-quantum roadmap, avoid public-key reuse, and keep signers ready to add post-quantum signature schemes as chains adopt them
authentication and identity (certificates, tokens, device attestation)Ed25519 (3)QSI-2026-19585Keep credentials short-lived and plan ML-DSA certificates, tokens and keys as the ecosystem supports them
role not determinedEd25519 (44), ECDSA (24), BLS12-381 (12), X25519 (9)QSI-2026-19577, QSI-2026-19578, QSI-2026-19584, QSI-2026-19586Classify each usage, record data lifetimes, and plan migration to Hybrid key establishment with ML-KEM (FIPS 203), e.g. X25519MLKEM768 in TLS 1.3 or mlkem768x25519-sha256 in SSH; introduce an abstraction layer for crypto-agility

Roles are judged from file paths, function names and the code around each match; review confirms them. Root-of-trust keys and wrapped keys come first: they are hard to replace or can be recorded today.

z is a planning assumption chosen per risk profile, not a prediction. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer is not publicly known to exist today.

Quantum algorithms relevant to this inventory

Quantum algorithmEffectInventoried algorithms (rows)What it means for this audit
Shor's algorithm — discrete logarithms in finite fields
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		breaks BLS12-381 (18)Breaks finite-field Diffie–Hellman and DSA at every size. Move key establishment to ML-KEM (hybrid with X25519 or ECDH during the transition) and signatures to ML-DSA or SLH-DSA.
Shor's algorithm — elliptic-curve discrete logarithms
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		breaks BLS12-381 (18), ECDSA (64), Ed25519 (76), X25519 (18)Elliptic-curve keys are expected to fall before RSA keys of comparable classical strength. On blockchains, coins whose public key is already on chain (reused addresses, pay-to-public-key and Taproot outputs) are exposed first; plan the move to post-quantum signatures and avoid key reuse in the meantime.
Grover's algorithm — key search and preimages
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		weakens (larger keys restore the margin) AES-256 (2), Argon2 (17), BLAKE2 (28), ChaCha20-Poly1305 (21), HMAC (16), Keccak-256 (8), MD5 (1), PBKDF2 (2), Poly1305 (18), SHA-2 (29), XSalsa20-Poly1305 (29), scrypt (3)Not a break. 256-bit keys (AES-256, ChaCha20) keep a comfortable margin; AES-128 meets NIST category 1, while some authorities ask for 256-bit keys in quantum-resistant contexts (see the AES-128 entry). Prefer 256-bit keys for long-lived data; 256-bit hashes need no change for preimage resistance.
Brassard–Høyer–Tapp — collision search
Q1: quantum computation offline, classical access to the victim		weakens (larger keys restore the margin) BLAKE2 (28), Keccak-256 (8), MD5 (1), SHA-2 (29)256-bit hashes (SHA-256, SHA3-256) remain adequate for collision resistance; 160-bit hashes are already weak classically (SHA-1 collisions are practical). Use 384/512-bit hashes where NIST categories 4–5 are required.

Effects: breaks — replace the algorithm; weakens — larger keys or outputs restore the margin; included in standard parameters — no action at standard parameter sets; only with superposition queries — not applicable to ordinary deployments.

QSI-2026-19587 · P1 · 30 daysroot-cause fix

Use the platform CSPRNG (secrets, os.urandom, crypto.getRandomValues, crypto/rand, SecureRandom, OsRng) or a hardware TRNG for every key, seed and mnemonic.

Rationale
Mnemonics, seeds or private keys drawn from such a generator can be enumerated from its small internal state: Milk Sad (CVE-2023-39910, mt19937 behind 'bx seed') and Trust Wallet (CVE-2023-31290) lost funds this way.
Expected outcome
Re-scan the source and review the call sites listed in the evidence.
Complexity
medium
Tests before change
Open line 59 in the supplied file src/crypto/SecretKey.h and inspect the quoted lines (see evidence).
Tests after change
Re-scan the source and review the call sites listed in the evidence.
Closure criteria
Re-scan the source and review the call sites listed in the evidence.

QSI-2026-19581 · P4 · 90 daysroot-cause fix

Plan migration of X25519 to Hybrid key establishment with ML-KEM (FIPS 203), e.g. X25519MLKEM768 in TLS 1.3 or mlkem768x25519-sha256 in SSH (or a hybrid scheme) once supported by your libraries, protocols and counterparties.

Rationale
Removes dependence on a quantum-vulnerable public-key primitive.
Expected outcome
The asset uses a NIST-standardized post-quantum or hybrid algorithm.
Complexity
high
Dependencies
Library/protocol support (e.g. OpenSSL ≥ 3.5, HSM firmware), interoperability with peers.
Side effects
Larger keys/signatures, possible performance and compatibility impact.
Tests before change
Interoperability tests in a staging environment.
Tests after change
Verify the negotiated/used algorithm on the production asset.
Closure criteria
Re-audit shows Hybrid key establishment with ML-KEM (FIPS 203), e.g. X25519MLKEM768 in TLS 1.3 or mlkem768x25519-sha256 in SSH or a hybrid scheme in use.
